title.en: Validate model moves while allowing honest previews

summary: Validate committed moves against the rules; distinguish accepted clamped candidates from rejected or cancelled previews.
objective: Keep interaction honest about which actions the puzzle rules permit.
applies_when: The user drags, slides or drops a piece under movement rules.
Some moves are blocked by other pieces or by the board.
Actions can be attempted rapidly or repeatedly.
intent_signals: why can I not move this
example_prompts: Let me slide the blocks with clear feedback when a move is blocked.
Stop pieces passing through each other.
negative_signals: Free placement sandboxes with no movement rules.
Physically simulated interactions, where contact rather than a rule set decides.
not_for: Free placement sandboxes with no movement rules.
Physically simulated interactions, where contact rather than a rule set decides.

principles: Committing a move to the model before it is validated produces a real illegal state, which teaches the wrong rules even if it is repaired afterwards. Showing an unaccepted move is different: a rejected preview, a resisted drag or a snap-back animation is honest as long as the model was never changed and the display makes the rejection obvious.
Silent refusal is equally poor: the user cannot distinguish an illegal move from an unresponsive interface, and will repeat the attempt.
Legality is often directional and path-dependent. A sliding piece must have every intermediate cell free, not just the destination, so the test must consider the path.
The rule set is part of the puzzle. Making refusals explain themselves teaches the rules through play instead of through instructions.
implementation: Evaluate the candidate move against the model, including its full path, before committing it. A visual preview may precede acceptance if it is clearly presented as a candidate.

Preview legality continuously during a drag, either by constraining the piece to legal positions or by showing the illegal candidate in a clearly rejected state; both are valid so long as releasing an illegal candidate changes nothing in the model.
Give refusals a specific reason and a specific location, such as the blocking piece, rather than a generic shake.
Define the policy for simultaneous or rapid input, and apply it consistently with the commit rule for accepted moves.
Keep the legality function shared between the interaction, any solver and any hint feature.
observable_checks: Attempt a move whose destination is free but whose path is blocked and confirm it is refused.

Drag against a wall and check the declared policy. Rejected or cancelled moves leave the model unchanged; a clamp-to-last-legal policy may commit that validated candidate on release, even when it differs from the starting cell. Preview appearance does not itself imply a commit.
Confirm every refusal produces feedback identifying the obstruction.
Compare the interaction result with the solver legality function on the same move.

creative_affordances: Refusal feedback can be playful, from resistance to sound to a highlighted blocker, as long as it is specific.
Rules that change during play are fine when the current rule set is discoverable.
known_limits: Authored interaction guidance; no runtime interaction has been exercised for this record.
It does not cover physically simulated contact, which is governed by a solver rather than a rule set.
